Laurens County sits in the Upstate, inside the Greenville-Anderson-Greer metro area. The city of Laurens serves as the seat and the largest community, and Clinton is the second main town. The 2020 census found 67,539 residents, with about 64 percent in rural areas.

A farmhouse outside Gray Court and a bungalow in town are taxed by the same offices yet attract different buyers. Older housing is common, from mill-era houses to farm property handed down through generations. An inherited house tends to come with an unpaid tax bill, a muddy title or no occupant, and any of these can hold up a closing.

Property tax runs through four county offices, and each answers a different question.

  • Assessor, 864-984-6546: appraises real property and answers legal residence questions.
  • Auditor, 864-984-2535: figures the tax and processes exemption paperwork.
  • Treasurer: takes payments, but neither sets amounts nor keeps owner records.
  • Tax Collector, 864-984-4742: handles accounts still unpaid after the March deadline.

Because the Treasurer holds no owner records, a bill sent to a stale address can go astray. After inheriting or buying a house, notify the Assessor of your address. Rate increases originate with County Council, the school board and municipal councils, which set their own revenue needs, and not with the Treasurer.

Pay by January 15 and no penalty applies. A weekend or holiday on that date extends the deadline to 5:00 p.m. the next business day, and the county must mail bills 30 or more days in advance.

DateWhat happens
January 15Last day to pay without penalty
After January 153 percent penalty under S.C. Code 12-45-180
February 2Further 7 percent penalty
March 17Further 5 percent penalty, and the Treasurer may issue a tax execution
After March 16Account goes to the Tax Collector

These stack up, which means a bill that sits into March is 15 percent bigger before collection costs. Many problem accounts on inherited houses started with a bill nobody opened in January.

Object by letter to the Assessor, and do it within 90 days of the day the notice went out. Your grounds may be fair market value, special use value or the assessment ratio.

A written notice is required by state law in only two cases: the Assessor raised a value by $1,000 or more, or taxed a property for the first time. If you never received one, a written appeal can be filed at any time. Filing ahead of the first penalty date applies the appeal to the current tax year, and filing on or after it applies to the next.

Call the Assessor at 864-984-6546 for the form and next step, and ask which balance stays protected while an appeal is open before you hold back any payment.

In South Carolina a legal residence is assessed at 4 percent of fair market value, while other real property is assessed at 6 percent. A house that does not pass the legal residence test is assessed at one and a half times the owner-occupied ratio.

S.C. Code 12-43-220 attaches these conditions to the 4 percent ratio:

  • Title is held by the owner, who lives there as a legal residence.
  • A sworn certification, under penalty of perjury, says no one in the household takes the ratio on a different home.
  • Rental use stays at 72 days or fewer in a calendar year.
  • After a sale the buyer files a new application, and the seller notifies the assessor within six months.

An application is due before the first penalty date of the year the ratio is first claimed. A fall closing that misses it leaves the buyer at 6 percent for the year.

The homestead exemption is a separate benefit. It removes the first $50,000 of a legal residence's fair market value for owners who are 65 or older, certified totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind, and the Auditor takes the applications.

Chapter 51 of Title 12 governs the delinquent tax sale, which the Delinquent Tax Collector's office runs. For twelve months after the sale, the owner may redeem.

The sale list is published in the Laurens County Advertiser and the Clinton Chronicle. The Forfeited Land Commission gets the opening bid, and bidders must register beforehand and attend in person. A tax deed follows within 45 days once the redemption period ends. Because sale dates change yearly, call 864-984-4742 for the current one.

S.C. Code 12-51-90 sets redemption interest as a share of the bid, stepping up each quarter: 3 percent for months 1 to 3, 6 percent for months 4 to 6, 9 percent for months 7 to 9 and 12 percent for months 10 to 12. Redemption is open to the owner in default, a grantee of the owner, and a mortgage or judgment creditor.

At the closing table, the title company normally pays the year's tax, drawing any unpaid balance from the seller's proceeds. Penalties shift on fixed dates, so request the exact payoff from the Treasurer or Tax Collector just before you close.

Sellers in this county keep running into the same few problems:

  • A bill mailed to a deceased parent's address and never opened.
  • Penalties that began January 16 and kept growing into March.
  • A legal residence ratio that lapsed after a move, so the 6 percent ratio applied.
  • An older house with repairs a mortgage lender would refuse to finance.

An owner carrying unpaid tax or needing repairs may choose an as-is cash sale. The tax is paid from the proceeds at closing, which means no cash up front is needed to clear it. A cash buyer is not tied to a lender's repair demands, so the closing date can follow your own schedule. Get any payoff figure in writing before you commit to a plan.

Bring the deed, the latest bill and your photo ID when you visit an office, and ask the Assessor to update the mailing address on the account if the buyer will receive the next bill.

A house that came through an estate raises the same questions in most cases, and the answers are simple to collect.

  1. Find the tax bills. Check the old address first, because the Treasurer keeps no owner records and mail may have gone there.
  2. Ask the Assessor to correct the address, and ask whether the legal residence ratio is still on the account or lapsed after the owner moved or died.
  3. Call the Tax Collector if the account is delinquent, and ask whether a sale date has been set.
  4. Gather the estate paperwork so the title company can clear the deed.

With those four answers in hand, you know what is owed, who to pay and how long you have, and you can decide between listing the house and selling it as-is for cash.

faqs.q: When are Laurens County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Penalty-free through January 15. When that date is a weekend or holiday, you have until 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a delinquent Laurens County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Collector, 864-984-4742. Past-due accounts move to that office after March 16.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Laurens County assessment?
faqs.a: Yes, by written objection to the Assessor, filed within 90 days of the notice's mailing date. The form is available at 864-984-6546.

faqs.q: Which Laurens County homes are taxed at 4 percent?
faqs.a: A legal residence only. Everything else is at 6 percent, and renting out the home more than 72 days a year can forfeit the lower ratio.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem a Laurens County house after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Twelve months from the sale date under state law. Interest rises from 3 to 12 percent of the bid, depending on which quarter you redeem in.
